Tempranillo takes its name from temprano, Spanish for early: it ripens weeks before Garnacha in the same vineyard.
Chablis and Champagne grow on the same seabed: Kimmeridgian limestone, full of fossilised oysters, runs under both.
A wine's legs, the streaks that run down the glass after a swirl, come from alcohol and sugar, not from quality.
Tannin is why red wine suits steak: it binds to the proteins and fat in the meat, so each sip tastes fresh again.
Rosé is made from red grapes whose skins are pulled away after a few hours; the longer they stay, the deeper the pink.
Champagne's bubbles come from a second fermentation inside the bottle, which is why the cork is held down with a wire cage.
Shiraz and Syrah are one grape: Australia kept the older name, France the one that stuck everywhere else.
Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape too; the Italian name usually means a lighter, crisper style.
Oak barrels give wine vanilla, toast and spice because the staves are charred over a flame when the barrel is made.
A corked wine smells of damp cardboard; the culprit is a compound called TCA, and a screwcap can't carry it.
Old vines give smaller crops, which is why the words vieilles vignes or old vine on a label usually mean more concentration.
Port is sweet because brandy is added mid-ferment: the spirit stops the yeast before it has eaten all the sugar.
Sherry's flor is a living layer of yeast that floats on the wine and keeps the air off it for years.
Amarone is made from grapes dried on racks for months, which is why it tastes so rich and reaches such high alcohol.
Sauternes owes its sweetness to a mould, noble rot, that shrivels the grapes and concentrates their sugar.
Rioja's Reserva and Gran Reserva are legal terms: they set a minimum number of years in oak and bottle before release.
Barolo and Barbaresco are both Nebbiolo from Piedmont; Barbaresco's slightly warmer sites ripen earlier and age sooner.
The dimple in the bottom of a bottle, the punt, was there to make hand-blown glass stable; it says nothing about quality.
Decanting a young red softens its tannins by giving it air; decanting an old one is mostly about leaving the sediment behind.
Red wine served too warm tastes soupy and alcoholic; most reds show best a little below room temperature.
Acidity is what makes your mouth water after a sip, and it's why crisp whites go so well with salty, fried or rich food.
Grenache is the world's most planted red grape you rarely see named: it hides inside Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Priorat and most Rioja blends.
New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc's passion-fruit punch comes from the same compounds found in the fruit itself.
Vintage Champagne is made only in years the house thinks are good enough; non-vintage blends several years for consistency.
Sulphites are in every wine, including organic ones: yeast makes them during fermentation, with or without a winemaker's help.
Malbec was a blending grape in Bordeaux before Argentina's high, dry vineyards turned it into a star on its own.
The Douro's Port vineyards are terraced by hand into slate so steep that a tractor would tip over.
Riesling can be bone dry or honey sweet from the same vineyard; the German word Trocken on the label means dry.
A wine's colour comes from the skins, so a white can be made from red grapes if the juice is pressed off quickly.
Pétillant naturel, or pét-nat, is bottled before its first fermentation finishes, so it makes its own gentle fizz.
